title: The Shape of a Coding Session
description: Nine new tools treat the coding session itself as the thing to design: where it lives, how it survives a reboot, and who gets to reshape it.

images.alt: A developer workspace with several terminal panes open side by side
images.caption: The session itself has become the unit of design, not just the model behind it.

content:
# The Shape of a Coding Session

For a long time a coding agent session was a simple thing: one transcript, one terminal window, one process that ended when you closed the tab. That assumption has quietly stopped holding. The nine tools in this group do not try to make a model smarter. They argue about the container the model runs in: how many sessions you can see at once, whether a workspace survives a reboot, whether a session can fork, clear itself, or be reached from a phone. It is infrastructure work, and it is where a surprising amount of the recent energy in developer tooling has gone.

## Where a session actually lives

The most direct answer is a smaller terminal. [[link:/tools/2293|Lmux]] is a native macOS terminal built in Swift on libghostty, a 25 MB app that idles near zero percent CPU with roughly ten settings. Its pitch is deliberately narrow: a terminal is still text in, text out, and the extra browser engines and workspace features that accumulated elsewhere are not wanted here. What it adds instead is agent awareness. Status arrives from Claude Code hooks and from Codex itself, so a pane can show running, needs you, done or failed, and one shortcut jumps to whoever is waiting. It never wraps claude or codex; it only listens. That restraint also lets it offer a rewind control that takes back a single turn without restarting a session.

[[link:/tools/2292|Synaps]] goes the other direction and rebuilds the runtime. It is a terminal-native agent runtime written in Rust, distributed as a single binary of about 32 MB, with interactive chat, parallel agent orchestration and autonomous supervision. The interesting part is provider plumbing rather than the chat loop: you can sign in with a Claude or GitHub Copilot subscription, pass a static API key, or point at a local Ollama model, and models are addressed as provider-qualified names. Cloud routes through Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex are text-only for now, and the runtime says so up front instead of failing halfway through a tool-using task.

Where one terminal is not enough, the session becomes a room. [[link:/tools/2294|SpaceApp]] is a self-hosted workspace that runs OpenCode, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini and a dozen more coding CLIs concurrently in persistent rooms on your own machine, installed with one command on Linux, macOS or Windows 11. Its Nous layer reads progress reports from each pane rather than scraping screens, so it can tell you what every agent is doing and bring you only the decisions that need you. The same rooms, panes and agents are then reachable from a phone or tablet. The documentation is careful to note that rooms organize sessions and are not a security boundary between mutually untrusted users, which is the kind of caveat worth reading before you invite a whole team in.

[[link:/tools/2295|CleanCode]] takes the spatial metaphor furthest. It calls itself a canvas ADE, an agentic development environment that puts agents, terminals and project workspaces on one canvas with stacking, grid layout and automatic organization. It supports 33 agent CLIs, and its own MCP lets agents operate the canvas, build workflows, create other agents and assign tasks. Branch workspaces use git worktrees so each branch gets its own canvas and terminals. The design is explicit about the division of labour: people handle fast intuitive judgment while agents handle the analysis, planning and tool learning. It is still labeled a preview, but the idea that a development environment should be a visible graph of concurrent work rather than a stack of tabs is now shared by several of these projects.

## Making a session survive

A session that fills its context window is a session that ends, and [[link:/tools/2297|Aigent-OS]] refuses to accept that. It is an MIT-licensed Claude Code harness that replaces automatic compaction with clear and resume. At a configurable threshold, 80 percent by default, it asks Claude to write a resume-ready checkpoint file called a capsule, waits for confirmation that the capsule is complete, sends exactly one clear, checks that a fresh session started, then tells the new session to load the capsule and carry on. No confirmation, no clear. The notes, decisions and open threads are plain markdown kept in git, so you can read, diff and roll back what your agent remembers. It runs locally on Node 18 or newer, has no server of its own, and ships a Codex adapter.

If a session can be forked, someone has to draw the fork tree. [[link:/tools/2298|Arvre]] is a terminal graph of Claude Code sessions and their forks, letting you navigate parents and children, resume a session, or copy a ready-made resume command to the clipboard. The clever detail is that Claude Code does not record a parent link when you fork, so Arvre infers it by linking each session to the earlier session that shares the most message IDs. That also explains its main weakness, stated plainly in the README: session data comes from an undocumented format that a future release could change. Installing it takes one pipx command on macOS and Linux.

[[link:/tools/2299|Cordane]] answers a different persistence question, which is how to reach your agents when the machine is behind a firewall. It is a self-hostable control plane where workers run on hardware you own and dial out to a hub over a single outbound connection, so there are no inbound ports, no VPN and no SSH configuration. Real PTYs survive closing the laptop, network drops and hub restarts, and two people can attach to the same live terminal. A files menu browses the machine, downloads a file or a whole folder and accepts uploads. It is free forever and self-hosted, though running a ticket still requires a supported coding CLI installed and logged in, and the tmux-like space layout is offered as an alternative rather than a drop-in replacement.

## Rewriting the harness itself

Two of the group treat the harness as material you are expected to reshape. [[link:/tools/2296|Uji]] is a coding agent where everything is a module, so you can swap any of them at runtime, even the core, and every view is Lua you can rewrite. It starts small and you add plugins as you go, and it installs through curl, Homebrew or a Fedora COPR repository. It is GPLv3 software and the README is short, which tells you roughly who it is for: people who intend to read the source rather than configure a product.

[[link:/tools/2300|Jauvex]] is an Electron desktop app that puts Claude Code, Codex and Grok sessions side by side and lets you steer them by voice. Its voice channel answers in three beats, a quick word, what it understood, then a summary of the agent answer, and it can steer a working agent without interrupting it or let agents talk to each other inside the app. There is no server; the window talks to the main process over IPC, and sessions stay where those CLIs already keep them. It is Apache 2.0 and builds from source on install, so nothing prebuilt is downloaded.

## What this changes

None of these tools improve a benchmark score. What they change is the unit of work. When a session can persist, fork, resume from a checkpoint, or be reached from another device, the natural length of a task grows, and the cost of losing context falls. That in turn makes it reasonable to run several agents at once, which creates the second-order problem these tools are also solving: knowing which one needs you, and proving later what each one did. The security and audit tools that appeared alongside this batch are a direct consequence. A session that never ends needs a record.

There is a common tradeoff too. Almost every one of these projects is self-hosted, local-first or open source, and almost every one asks you to install language servers, run a hub, commit a map file, or accept an unsigned binary. The control is real, but so is the setup. That is a reasonable exchange for a tool that will sit underneath your working day, and it is worth noticing how few of these launches are pitched as a hosted service. The session, apparently, is something developers still want to keep on their own machine.
tldr: Synaps, Lmux, SpaceApp, CleanCode, Uji, Aigent-OS, Arvre, Cordane and Jauvex all redesign the container a coding agent runs in rather than the model inside it.
